title: New Year's resolutions and the myth of self-control
subtitle: Self-control is strategy, not willpower
author: Matthew C. Haug
introduction: Keeping your New Year's resolutions is not about how much willpower you have. New research suggests the most self-controlled people don't rely on willpower, but prevent irresistible desires from emerging by creating environments where temptations simply don’t arise. By controlling our environment, rather than by attempting to control ourselves, we can keep our actions in line with our goals – and maybe even stick to our resolutions this year.
body:
Each year, millions of people make New Year’s resolutions, with goals like exercising more, saving more money, losing weight, improving one’s diet, and spending less time on social media among the most popular in recent years. However, it seems that most people fail to keep their resolutions for very long, with some studies suggesting that by six months about 60% of individuals fail to maintain their commitments and that about 80% have failed after two years.

Making significant changes to patterns in your daily life is hard, and there are many reasons that people fail to achieve what they resolve to do. For example, you may set an unrealistic or overly general goal or set a realistic goal but fail to outline intermediate steps to achieve it. Yet, even if you avoid these problems, there will be times when you are faced with potential temptations to break your resolution: to sleep in instead of going to the gym, to buy that expensive latte instead of saving a bit of money, to eat a second piece of cheesecake instead of sticking to your diet. To keep a resolution for any significant amount of time, you need self-control.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The politics of desire With Barry C. Smith, Zoe Strimpel, Maya Oppenheim, Kimberly McIntosh

But what is self-control, and how can we be more self-controlled if we find ourselves too easily doing things that we judge not to be in our best interest? I’ll outline reasons to think that some longstanding assumptions about self-control are misguided and that standard categories of self-control fail to map onto actual human psychology. Abandoning, or radically revising, these assumptions and categories may help us better understand what our self-control capacities are like and how they can be improved.

In recent decades, philosophical work on self-control has focused on self-control as a psychological state—exercising self-control at a particular moment in time. Much of this work tries to resolve puzzles posed by a particular kind of state self-control—synchronic self-control, which occurs when you exercise self-control against a simultaneous desire that conflicts with your evaluative judgment about what it is best to do. (Call this a simultaneous “conflicting desire” for short.) However, if we are interested in the kind of self-control involved in keeping a resolution for months or years, it seems that we should also investigate what it is to be a self-controlled person—what is involved in having a high-level of self-control as a psychological trait.

One common conception of trait self-control traces back to the Aristotelian notion of enkrateia, literally “empowered [over oneself],” which is usually translated as “continence”—a term for self-restraint or holding back that now unfortunately is mainly used in ordinary speech to refer to control over one’s excretory functions. Enkratic people regularly experience conflicting desires, but they are good at directly resisting or inhibiting those desires in the moment. So, an enkratic person who is committed to eating a healthy diet will regularly want to eat junk food but will usually successfully resist these desires.

Much work on self-control has assumed that it is enkrateia, and this conceptionhas at least implicitly influenced what has been the dominant model of self-control in social and personality psychology until very recently: the “resource” or “strength” model, which takes self-control to be a limited resource or muscle that is depleted from overuse and can be strengthened through training and practice. On this model, highly self-controlled people have lots of willpower and are good at using it to directly resist tempting desires.

Highly self-controlled people seem to be good at selecting and modifying their environments so that they are less likely to face strong temptations.

However, a growing body of empirical evidence suggests that people who score highly on measures of trait self-control are not enkratic—they are not particularly strong-willed, i.e., not particularly good at directly resisting their conflicting desires. Instead, highly self-controlled people seem to be good only at using indirect strategies to prevent such strong impulses from occurring in the first place. That is, highly self-controlled people seem to be good at selecting and modifying their environments so that they are less likely to face strong temptations. For example, they might delete their social media apps from their phone if they want to spend less time doomscrolling. Highly self-controlled people may also be good at using psychological strategies to reconstrue, or direct their attention from, tempting alternatives so that they do not experience strong desires to pursue those alternatives. For example, if a highly self-controlled person believes that he should not eat another cookie, he might think of it as a slab of fat to make it less attractive.

In short, enkrateia requires having a significant number of occurrent conflicting desires and a strong will to directly resist these desires. Highly self-controlled people seem to have neither of these features. This is one reason to reject the traditional model of trait self-control as enkrateia.

A defender of the traditional model might point out that enkrateia can also be exercised by using indirect self-control strategies to prevent foreseeable conflicting desires from becoming occurrent. This is true, but having an excellent ability to use indirect self-control strategies is not enough to make one enkratic.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Ancient traits in the modern world With Sunetra Gupta, Anders Sandberg, Subrena Smith, Güneş Taylor

To see this, it will help to contrast enkrateia with another Aristotelian category related to self-control: sophrosyne, typically translated as “temperance” or “moderation,” an ability to strike the right balance or to keep things in due measure or proportion. Sophrosyne is one of the four cardinal virtues—along with wisdom, courage, and justice—that originate in ancient Greek thought. While the enkraticperson is often tempted but is good at resisting those temptations, the sophron individual isn’t tempted in the first place; their occurrent desires are always in harmony with their evaluative judgments about what they should do. So, for example, a sophron person who is committed to healthy eating will never have an occurrent desire to eat junk food when she believes she should not eat it.

Paradigmatically sophron individuals have appetitive and affective capacities that in themselves tend to conform to their evaluative judgments. This is why many thinkers have supposed that sophrosyne is an intrinsically better trait than enkrateia: it has seemed to many that living a life free from psychological turmoil or conflict is better than having to overcome such conflict to do what one judges best. Yet sophrosyne is compatible with having some foreseeable motivational conflict. The sophron individual is not completely insensible to the tempting things for which less moderate people sometimes have strong occurrent desires. So, there are some situations in which the sophron individual can rightly expect that she would have strong occurrent conflicting desires, and she can take steps to avoid these situations or use other indirect self-control strategies to ward off the use of direct willpower.

This is why having an excellent ability to use indirect self-control strategies to prevent foreseeable conflicting desires from becoming occurrent is not sufficient for enkrateia. For, having such an ability is also involved in sophrosyne, and enkrateia and sophrosyne are mutually exclusive traits. An individual cannot have both at once. Yet being able to use indirect self-control strategies successfully is a feature involved in each of these traits.

One might suggest that the empirical evidence mentioned above is compatible with high trait self-control simply being sophrosyne rather than enkrateia. Yet it’s not clear that highly self-controlled individuals exactly fit the traditional conception of sophrosyne, either. For one thing, if you are highly self-controlled you may need to use indirect strategies to prevent occurrent motivational conflict far more often that a paradigmatically sophron individual would. What’s more, highly self-controlled people may have standing motivations to pursue tempting alternatives that are so strong that they must rely on indirect strategies to achieve harmony between their occurrent desires and their evaluative judgments. By contrast, as I noted above, paradigmatically sophron individuals tend to have motivational dispositions that result in their occurrent desires conforming to their evaluative judgments without their needing to make any additional strategic interventions.

If you struggle with succumbing to temptation, it may be better to work on developing indirect strategies to prevent strong conflicting desires from arising.

The upshot is that excellent trait self-control seems to be a trait that is intermediate between enkrateia and sophrosyne. Let’s call it “indirect harmony.” Like both enkrateia and sophrosyne, indirect harmony involves an excellent ability to use indirect self-control strategies to ensure that the desires on which one acts conform to one’s evaluative practical judgments. However, unlike enkrateia, indirect harmony need not (and typically does not) consist in having exceptional willpower. Further, unlike sophrosyne, the motivational dispositions of those with indirect harmony need not be, in themselves, almost always in line with their evaluative judgments.

If indirect harmony is a better model for being a self-controlled person than either enkrateia or sophrosyne, then this may provide guidance on how to stick to one’s resolutions. If you struggle with succumbing to temptation, it may be better to work on developing indirect strategies to prevent strong conflicting desires from arising, instead of berating yourself for lacking willpower and trying to build up your ability to directly resist those strong desires. Even if sophrosyne—“the harmonious product of intense passion under perfect control,” as Helen North has described it—is an ideal toward which we should strive, it is likely that exhibiting indirect harmony is a good way to work toward that ideal.

Alternatively, it may be that extensive use of indirect self-control strategies is itself how we humans can best keep intense passion under “perfect control.” In that case, indirect harmony would simply be what human virtue with respect to appetite and affect looks like. Further collaborative work between philosophers and mind scientists is needed to investigate the fine structure of human self-control-related capacities and the ways in which these capacities contribute to, and perhaps in some cases detract from, individual and societal well-being.
